findings.explanation: There are eleven declared overloads: String, Reader, and JsonElement each have Class<T>, Type, and TypeToken<T> forms; JsonReader has only Type and TypeToken<T> forms. Each Class overload delegates through TypeToken.get(classOfT) without an explicit return cast. Each Type overload delegates through TypeToken.get(typeOfT) and applies an unchecked `(T)` return cast. String/TypeToken checks for Java null, wraps non-null text in StringReader, and calls Reader/TypeToken. Reader/TypeToken creates a configured JsonReader, calls the common JsonReader/TypeToken implementation, then checks full consumption. JsonElement/TypeToken checks for Java null, wraps a non-null tree in JsonTreeReader, and calls the same core implementation. Although no JsonReader/Class overload is declared, a call such as fromJson(reader, Foo.class) selects fromJson(JsonReader, Type), because Class implements java.lang.reflect.Type; that overload then creates a TypeToken and performs its unchecked return cast.

A Java-null JsonElement returns Java null before constructing a JsonTreeReader, peeking, looking up an adapter, or reading. The equivalent String shortcut is in String/TypeToken and occurs before StringReader construction. Calls through a Class or Type overload first convert the valid target argument to a TypeToken and then reach the shortcut. Empty text is not this shortcut; it reaches the parser and may return null through the initial-EOF rule. JsonNull is a non-null JsonElement, so it is wrapped in JsonTreeReader and routed through the core: the initial peek observes a JSON NULL token, then the selected adapter reads it and its result is validated. Thus JsonNull does not itself force a Java-null result; that result is adapter-defined, and a custom adapter may return another value or throw.

String inputs route through Reader/TypeToken, so both perform this post-read check, but only after the core returns normally. For a non-null adapter result, END_DOCUMENT passes; any returned token means remaining data and produces the message-only JsonSyntaxException shown. This establishes only that nothing remains: a custom adapter that consumes multiple top-level values and reaches the end can pass. If the adapter returns null—even after consuming nothing or leaving trailing data—the condition short-circuits and no completion peek occurs. The same skip applies to the null returned for initially empty input. A MalformedJsonException raised by the completion peek becomes JsonSyntaxException with that exception as cause; any other IOException, including an EOFException at this phase, becomes JsonIOException with its cause. Other runtime exceptions and errors are not caught here. Direct JsonReader entry points perform one adapter call with no completion check, leaving any trailing token untouched. JsonElement entry points likewise call the core directly without this check; although a tree has one root, a custom adapter's partial or absent consumption is not verified.

A newly constructed JsonReader defaults to LEGACY_STRICT, and Gson.newJsonReader explicitly selects the Gson instance's configured strictness or LEGACY_STRICT when none was configured. In the core, any explicit Gson setting—including explicitly selected LEGACY_STRICT—overrides an existing reader's setting for adapter reading. Without an explicit Gson setting, an existing LEGACY_STRICT reader is temporarily changed to LENIENT, an already-LENIENT reader remains LENIENT, and a STRICT reader remains STRICT. JsonTreeReader also enters this same selection logic. The finally block restores the exact old setting after initial peek, adapter lookup/read, result validation, and all normal or exceptional exits from that try, including the empty-input return and uncaught runtime exceptions. For String/Reader entry points, restoration happens before assertFullConsumption: with default Gson settings, adapter parsing is LENIENT but the newly created reader has already been restored to LEGACY_STRICT for the trailing-data peek; with explicit strictness, that configured value is restored and used there. Direct JsonReader and tree entry points have no later completion phase.

The core first peeks, discarding the returned token; only after that succeeds does it mark the input non-empty, look up the adapter for the complete TypeToken, invoke exactly one adapter read, and validate the returned object. The adapter itself may consume zero, one, or multiple values. A null result bypasses type validation and is returned. For a non-null result, the requested raw class is primitive-wrapped, so an int request accepts Integer, for example. Class.isInstance tests assignability, not exact class identity, so subclasses and interface implementations are accepted. Because only the raw type is tested, generic contents are not validated—for example, a List<Integer> can satisfy the runtime check for a requested List<String>. A non-assignable result causes the detailed ClassCastException before any Reader-level completion check; that exception is not caught by the core, though strictness is still restored in finally.

isEmpty remains true only until the initial peek returns. Therefore an EOFException thrown by that initial peek is treated as the empty-document signal and returns null. Once the peek returns successfully, isEmpty is false; any later EOFException, normally from adapter reading after partial input, becomes JsonSyntaxException with the EOFException as cause. A peek that returns END_DOCUMENT is a successful peek, not the initial-EOF shortcut: adapter lookup and reading are still attempted, so a custom adapter may return a value or null, while a typical adapter may fail; any resulting behavior then follows the normal validation and catch rules. During this parse phase, IllegalStateException and every non-EOF IOException—including MalformedJsonException and underlying Reader failures—become JsonSyntaxException with the original cause. AssertionError is replaced by a new AssertionError whose message is prefixed with the Gson version and whose cause is the original error. ClassCastException, other RuntimeException types, and Errors other than AssertionError escape unchanged, while finally still restores strictness. The later full-consumption peek is outside this catch block: malformed JSON there maps to JsonSyntaxException, other I/O maps to JsonIOException, and AssertionError is not version-decorated.

findings.explanation: There are 11 declared overloads: String × {Class<T>, Type, TypeToken<T>}; Reader × the same three; JsonReader × {Type, TypeToken<T>}; and JsonElement × {Class<T>, Type, TypeToken<T>}. Every Class overload delegates through TypeToken.get(Class); every Type overload delegates through TypeToken.get(Type) and performs an explicit unchecked (T) return cast. A non-null String is wrapped in StringReader and handed to the Reader/TypeToken overload shown here. That overload creates a configured JsonReader, invokes the common JsonReader/TypeToken implementation, and then checks full consumption. A JsonElement is wrapped in JsonTreeReader and sent directly to that same common implementation. There is deliberately no JsonReader/Class overload. Because Class implements java.lang.reflect.Type, fromJson(jsonReader, SomeClass.class) selects the JsonReader/Type overload, whose T is inferred from the call context rather than constrained by a Class<T> parameter; it then creates a token with TypeToken.get(Type), uses the common implementation, and applies the unchecked return cast.

Java-null String and JsonElement inputs are entry-point shortcuts. Their Class or Type overload first converts the valid target to a TypeToken and delegates; the TypeToken overload then returns null. For String, this happens before constructing StringReader, so there is no JsonReader, adapter lookup, parsing, validation, or completion check. The quoted tree check likewise occurs before constructing JsonTreeReader. JsonNull is a non-null JsonElement and therefore does not take this shortcut: it is wrapped in JsonTreeReader and passed through initial peek, adapter lookup, adapter read, and result validation. The entry point itself does not mandate that JsonNull—or textual JSON null—become Java null; the selected adapter controls that result.

Every non-null String routes through Reader, and Reader/TypeToken calls this helper after the common parse returns. Direct JsonReader and JsonElement entry points do not call it, so they do not reject data left by an adapter. Even for String/Reader, this is only an end-position check, not proof that exactly one value was consumed: an adapter that consumes multiple values and reaches END_DOCUMENT passes. If the adapter returns null—including a custom adapter returning null without consuming anything—the condition short-circuits and trailing input is never inspected. For a non-null result, a successfully returned token other than END_DOCUMENT produces the message-only JsonSyntaxException shown. A MalformedJsonException from the completion peek becomes JsonSyntaxException with the malformed exception as cause; any other IOException, including an EOFException at this phase, becomes JsonIOException with that cause. If the core parse fails or result validation fails, this post-check is never reached.

JsonReader itself defaults to LEGACY_STRICT, and Gson.newJsonReader explicitly selects the Gson instance's configured strictness or LEGACY_STRICT when none was configured. In the common entry point, an explicit Gson strictness overrides any existing reader setting. Without an explicit Gson setting, an existing LEGACY_STRICT reader is temporarily changed to LENIENT; existing LENIENT and STRICT settings remain unchanged. A finally block restores oldStrictness on normal return, empty-input return, translated failure, and uncaught failures arising inside the parse try. For String/Reader, restoration occurs before control returns to the Reader overload and before assertFullConsumption runs. Consequently, an unconfigured newly created reader parses the value temporarily as LENIENT but performs the trailing-data peek after restoration to LEGACY_STRICT; explicit strictness remains in effect for both phases. Direct JsonReader and tree calls have restoration but no completion phase.

The common entry point first peeks, then marks the input non-empty after any successful peek, then looks up the adapter, invokes its read method, and finally validates the returned object. Thus an EOFException from the first peek prevents adapter lookup, while any returned token—including END_DOCUMENT—continues to lookup and read. Adapter consumption is not otherwise constrained here. A null adapter result is accepted for every requested raw type, including primitives, and skips validation. For a non-null result, primitive raw classes are wrapped first (for example, int is validated against Integer), then Class.isInstance performs an assignability check. Subclasses and interface implementations are accepted; exact-class equality is not required. Only the raw type is checked, so parameterized contents such as List<String> versus List<Integer> are not validated. A non-null raw-type mismatch throws the constructed ClassCastException; it is not caught by this method's catch clauses, though strictness is restored in finally.

isEmpty remains true only while the initial peek has not returned. An EOFException thrown by that initial peek is treated as an empty document: null is returned and the exception is discarded. If peek instead returns END_DOCUMENT, isEmpty becomes false and processing continues to adapter lookup/read; END_DOCUMENT is not an automatic null result. Any EOFException thrown later by adapter reading is therefore wrapped in JsonSyntaxException with the EOFException as cause. IllegalStateException and any other IOException arising in the parse try are likewise wrapped in JsonSyntaxException with the original exception as cause. An AssertionError is replaced with a new AssertionError whose message includes the Gson version and original message and whose cause is the original error. Other RuntimeExceptions—including the deliberate result-validation ClassCastException and adapter or lookup exceptions other than IllegalStateException—and Errors other than AssertionError are not caught and propagate after finally restores strictness. These catches cover the core parse try only. The later Reader/String completion peek has separate rules: END_DOCUMENT succeeds, MalformedJsonException becomes caused JsonSyntaxException, and other I/O—including EOFException—becomes caused JsonIOException; its runtime exceptions and AssertionErrors are not handled by this block.

JsonElement/TypeToken handles Java null, otherwise wraps the tree in JsonTreeReader and calls that same core parser directly. There is deliberately no JsonReader/Class overload. Consequently, `fromJson(jsonReader, Foo.class)` selects JsonReader/Type because Class implements Type; that method converts Foo.class to a TypeToken and uses Foo as the requested adapter/raw validation type. Its generic return T is target-typed independently of the Class argument, unlike the Class<T> overloads, so an inconsistent assignment can still incur a caller-side cast failure.

A Java-null JsonElement returns Java null before JsonTreeReader construction, peeking, adapter lookup, reading, validation, or any consumption check. Class and Type tree calls reach this shortcut only after converting their valid target to TypeToken. String behaves analogously: String/Class and String/Type first convert the target, then String/TypeToken returns null before constructing StringReader. Reader and direct JsonReader entry points have no analogous input shortcut (their inputs are assumed non-null here). JsonNull is different from a Java-null tree reference: it is a non-null JsonElement, is wrapped in JsonTreeReader, appears as a NULL token, and proceeds through adapter lookup and adapter.read. The adapter therefore determines whether JsonNull—or textual JSON `null`—produces Java null or some non-null value; a null result is accepted by the later validation.

String reaches Reader/TypeToken and therefore shares its post-parse completion check. The check runs only after the core parser returns normally. For a non-null result, END_DOCUMENT passes; any successfully peeked token instead produces JsonSyntaxException with the explicit message and no cause. A MalformedJsonException thrown by the completion peek becomes JsonSyntaxException with that exception as cause, while every other IOException—including an EOFException from a custom/overridden completion peek—becomes JsonIOException with the I/O exception as cause. Unchecked exceptions and errors from this phase are not caught here. Critically, when the adapter returns null, the condition does not even call peek: trailing data is accepted regardless of whether the adapter consumed one value, part of one, several values, or nothing. Empty-input null gets the same bypass. A non-null custom result only verifies the reader's resulting position; an adapter that consumes several top-level values can still pass if it leaves END_DOCUMENT. Direct JsonReader overloads intentionally perform no full-consumption check and can leave trailing tokens. JsonElement overloads also call the core JsonReader entry directly, so they do not validate that a custom adapter consumed the whole tree.

JsonReader itself defaults to LEGACY_STRICT, and Gson.newJsonReader explicitly chooses the Gson instance's configured strictness or LEGACY_STRICT when Gson has no explicit setting. During the core read, an explicit Gson setting overrides an existing reader's old LEGACY_STRICT, LENIENT, or STRICT value. Without an explicit Gson setting, an old LEGACY_STRICT reader is temporarily changed to LENIENT for backward compatibility, while an already-LENIENT or STRICT reader is left in that mode. The finally block restores the exact old value after success, an empty-input return, a caught failure, or an uncaught failure from inside the try. For String/Reader entry points this restoration happens before assertFullConsumption: with default Gson settings, adapter parsing is therefore LENIENT but the newly created reader is back to LEGACY_STRICT for the completion peek. With explicit strictness, both phases use that configured value. Direct JsonReader and tree entry points have no later completion phase, but still perform and restore the same temporary strictness selection.

The core first peeks, marks the input non-empty after any successful peek, then looks up the adapter for the complete TypeToken, invokes adapter.read, and only afterward validates the returned object. Thus an initial EOF can return before adapter lookup, while successful NULL and END_DOCUMENT peeks both continue to lookup/read. Adapter consumption is otherwise unchecked at this boundary. A null adapter result is accepted for every requested type, including primitive types. For non-null results, Gson wraps a primitive raw class—so, for example, Integer is valid for int—and applies Class.isInstance against the requested raw type. A mismatch throws the shown ClassCastException before any Reader full-consumption check. That exception is not among the core catches and escapes unchanged. The unchecked Type overload return casts also cannot make generic contents safe or tie target-typed T to a supplied Type argument.

isEmpty remains true only until the initial peek completes normally. An EOFException thrown by that initial peek is treated as an empty document and swallowed by returning null. After any successful peek, isEmpty is false, so an EOFException subsequently thrown by adapter lookup/read is wrapped in JsonSyntaxException with the EOFException as cause. A returned END_DOCUMENT token is not an exception and is not treated as the initial-empty shortcut: isEmpty becomes false and Gson still looks up and calls the adapter; the adapter may return null, return another value, or fail. Other RuntimeExceptions—including the explicit wrong-result ClassCastException and custom JsonSyntaxException/JsonIOException—and errors other than AssertionError are not caught and propagate unchanged; the finally restoration still runs. findings.explanation: The deprecated ByteString declaration maps `create(contentType, content)` directly to `content.toRequestBody(contentType)`. The adjacent String declaration performs the identical mapping to the String receiver extension. Thus Kotlin migration changes a content-type-first call into receiver form; the corresponding Java-facing order is content first and nullable content type second, namely `create(String, MediaType)` or `create(ByteString, MediaType)`. These delegates add no behavior of their own: String then follows charset selection and byte-array encoding, whereas ByteString preserves the supplied content type and writes its existing bytes directly.

The deprecated File form maps `create(contentType, file)` to `file.asRequestBody(contentType)`, making the file first in the Java-facing replacement. Its ByteArray sibling maps `create(contentType, content, offset, byteCount)` to `content.toRequestBody(contentType, offset, byteCount)`: content moves first while `offset` and `byteCount` retain their order and values. Its defaults also remain `offset = 0` and `byteCount = content.size`. Neither legacy declaration wraps or alters the replacement body.

Charset selection happens before encoding. The String is encoded once into a fresh ByteArray using the selected charset, then delegated as the complete slice `(offset = 0, byteCount = bytes.size)`. Consequently, the resulting content type is the helper's `finalContentType`, its length is the encoded byte count rather than the String's character count, and each write emits the retained encoded bytes without re-encoding the String.

For a null media type, the initial UTF-8 selection remains in force and the final content type remains null. A non-null media type with a supported charset uses that charset and preserves the original media type. A missing charset, or a charset name that is invalid or unsupported by the runtime, makes `MediaType.charset()` return null; all three cases therefore encode as UTF-8 and append `; charset=utf-8` to the media-type text. The augmented text is parsed with the nullable `toMediaTypeOrNull()`, so a parse failure yields a null final content type instead of throwing. Parameter lookup returns the first matching charset. Therefore, if the original type already had an invalid or unsupported charset, appending a second UTF-8 parameter does not override it: later charset lookup still encounters the original parameter first and again returns its default, normally null. This lookup result does not change the already-selected UTF-8 encoding.

The defaults select the entire array: offset zero and count equal to the full array size. The count default is not `size - offset`; consequently, supplying any nonzero offset while omitting count fails bounds validation. Validation occurs eagerly before the RequestBody is returned and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` for a negative offset/count, an offset past the end, or a count exceeding the bytes remaining from the offset. findings.explanation: Every Axios instance owns separate request and response managers, so each has an independent handlers array and ID namespace. use appends a record and returns its zero-based array index. With no/falsy options object, synchronous defaults to false and runWhen to null; with an options object, the corresponding property values are stored directly, so omitted properties become undefined. eject(id) replaces a currently present record with null: it does not splice, reuse, or renumber slots, and it returns undefined. Thus later registrations continue at the old array length. forEach visits slots in ascending order and skips null tombstones. clear replaces handlers with a fresh empty array, so iteration sees nothing and the next registration returns 0; because IDs are unversioned indexes, an old numeric ID can collide with a post-clear registration.

During _request assembly, every request runWhen function is evaluated against the same already-prepared config, before any request interceptor runs. Skipping requires the predicate result to be exactly false; other results remain eligible. The skip occurs before synchronous-mode accumulation, so skipped interceptors cannot affect mode. The flag starts true and ANDs only eligible request records: synchronous mode is selected when every eligible request interceptor has a truthy synchronous option, including the empty-eligible-set case; any eligible false/undefined option selects the Promise path. Manager iteration is registration order, but each eligible request pair is unshifted, yielding reverse-registration/LIFO request order while preserving fulfilled/rejected adjacency. Response pairs are pushed, yielding registration/FIFO order. Response runWhen and synchronous options are never consulted here and cannot affect mode selection.

If any eligible request interceptor is not synchronous, assembly starts with Promise.resolve(config), places reverse-registration request pairs before dispatch, and places registration-order response pairs after dispatch. The loop attaches every pair with then before callbacks begin running. A fulfilled callback's returned value becomes the next fulfillment, and a returned promise/thenable is adopted; a throw becomes the next rejection. A rejection callback can recover by returning a value, while a missing callback forwards the rejection and a throwing callback replaces it with the new error. Crucially, the rejected callback paired in the same then does not catch a throw from its own fulfilled callback: both consume the preceding promise, so that throw reaches the next pair's rejection callback. Consequently an unrecovered request failure skips dispatch and can reach response rejection handlers. Response handlers are already attached as downstream stages when dispatch eventually executes, so even a synchronous dispatch throw inside that Promise stage becomes a rejection visible to them. The public async request awaits the final chain and rethrows any rejection left unrecovered.

In synchronous mode, eligible request fulfilled callbacks execute directly and immediately, with each successful returned configuration replacing newConfig. Unlike the Promise path, the explicit catch invokes that interceptor's own paired rejection callback for its fulfilled callback's throw, with the Axios instance as receiver. The rejection callback's return value is ignored, the request loop always stops afterward, and—if it returns normally—dispatch proceeds with the last successfully assigned configuration. If the rejection callback is missing, onRejected.call itself throws a TypeError; if it throws, that replacement error escapes. Either case prevents dispatch and prevents response-handler attachment. The exact synchronous attachment boundary is successful return from dispatchRequest.call: only afterward are response then pairs attached. A synchronous dispatch throw instead takes the early Promise.reject return, bypassing all response interceptors; an asynchronously rejected promise returned by dispatch does pass through the subsequently attached response rejection handlers. The public async request catches/awaits both escaped synchronous errors and final promise rejections and rethrows the remaining reason.

note: Missing terminal artifacts are not evidence of a stopped process. No models are run or retried.
